label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.why: I have not been told yet what the team or its wakes are, so the four phases give me hours but nothing I can picture.

findings.quote: with each hour's commits and its wakes marked on it
findings.why: Wakes and commits are used here, but the word wake is only explained on the tour page, so a phone reader stalls on the first figure.

findings.quote: grouped into the setup, the flow, the acceleration and the crunch and the stop
findings.why: The figure line tells the four parts a second time, straight after the paragraph that names them.

findings.quote: my return, the talk growing, my words arriving faster than the clock
findings.why: The acceleration is the part a team like mine wants to understand, but it is described in a phrase I cannot decode yet.

findings.quote: Before I tell you how the factory worked
findings.why: I am not told what the factory is, who is in it or how it stops, which are the three things I came to learn.
This tells me how to read, where saying the agents' words are written for this book would do.

findings.quote: You meet each of them properly when they arrive, in the chapters that follow.
findings.why: Line 5 has already said one line from the agent that made each stop, so this repeats the promise.

findings.quote: This is the page that shows the factory running on its own for nine hours.
findings.why: The narrator reports what the page shows, with no I and no view from now about why it matters.

findings.quote: Read in order, they are the team talking.
findings.why: It is an instruction on how to read the commits and stands in for saying what I would find.

findings.quote: Last stop. Every agent has a page like this, built from its own folder.
findings.why: Reporting with no I and no hindsight, and two short sentences open it.

findings.quote: A key's fingerprint is a short code that identifies it.
findings.why: Keys, fingerprints and vaults arrive in one dense paragraph, and as a busy reader with a team to run I cannot see why I need them.

findings.quote: the same kind of key as a QR code
findings.why: The keys page figure and the QR figure show the same thing twice, and the paragraph above already says every key is public and on purpose.

findings.quote: That list is often shorter than you expect
findings.why: It predicts how the reader will find the exercise, and the takeaway is about explaining pages, not about running a team with agents, so I get a story but no pattern to copy.

findings.quote: And the historian made an error, and caught it itself.
findings.why: A run of short sentences lists failures one after another, with no sentence that runs on into what each taught.

findings.quote: the editions from one page up to this one
findings.why: I do not know what the editions are or which one I am reading, so the line stops me.

findings.quote: I left the times out of this page on purpose.
findings.why: It ends the page on what is missing, and a team member learns nothing here they could copy tomorrow.

what_holds: 03-the-tour.md: four stops, each with one picture and one line from an agent, is quick to take in on a phone and shows a finished thing first.
03-the-tour.md: the plain definitions of wake, conductor and hold (line 41) are what I needed, and the researcher admitting the counts disagree (line 61) builds trust.
03-the-tour.md: the rules-carry-their-mistakes idea at Stop 4 is something I could copy tomorrow.
94-the-making-of-this-book.md: the failures stay in (the hold, the lost evening, the historian's error), which makes the account believable.
notes: The three sections never say how the team stops or what one person would start with tomorrow; the hold is mentioned in the tour, but only as a dashboard item. The makers-of-this-book page would serve me better with one takeaway line I could act on.
